The curve starts at \(\Omega_t = 0\) when \(\Omega = 0\), rises to a peak of \(\pi\) at \(\Omega = \pi/2\), and then decreases back to \(0\) when \(\Omega = \pi\). This mapping is characteristic of a frequency transformation that maps the entire baseband \(0 \le \Omega \le \pi\) to a band around \(\pi/2\). Specifically, the low frequencies near \(\Omega = 0\) and the high frequencies near \(\Omega = \pi\) are mapped to low frequencies near \(\Omega_t = 0\), while the mid-frequencies near \(\Omega = \pi/2\) are mapped to high frequencies near \(\Omega_t = \pi\). When a low-pass filter (which passes frequencies near \(\Omega = 0\) and blocks frequencies near \(\Omega = \pi\)) is subjected to this transformation, the passband near \(\Omega = 0\) is mapped to a passband near \(\Omega_t = 0\), and the stopband near \(\Omega = \pi\) is also mapped to a stopband near \(\Omega_t = 0\). The frequencies that were previously in the stopband (near \(\pi/2\)) are now mapped to the passband (near \(\pi\)). Thus, the resulting filter passes low frequencies (near 0) and high frequencies (near \(\pi\)), while blocking mid-frequencies (near \(\pi/2\)). This is the definition of a band-stop filter.
